question: Within the framework of the EU’s customs reform, the exemption from customs duties for consignments valued below EUR 150 will be abolished. However, the framework does not appear to introduce any meaningful distinction between product categories, meaning that fastfashion items from non-EU countries, books, or press products may all fall under the same customs duties and related fees.
As a result, situations may arise in which even low-value newspapers or magazines are subject to the same flat-rate charge and handling fee as other imported goods of similar value.

Given that cultural goods – in particular books, newspapers and periodicals – are essential for access to information, media pluralism and cultural diversity, it is questionable whether the current design of the rules adequately reflects the specific nature and societal value of these products. I would therefore like to ask the Commission the following: 1.
Does it intend to consider any measures for cultural and educational goods – particularly books and newspapers – in relation to handling and administrative fees affected by the Customs Union reform?
Has the Commission taken into account existing global practices that provide customs or fee exemptions or reductions for cultural goods, in particular books and press products?
answer: Within the context of the EU Customs Reform, Council Regulation (EU) 2026/382 abolishes the EUR 150 threshold-based customs duty exemption and imposes, from 1 July 2026 until 1 July 2028, a temporary EUR 3 customs duty per item in consignments valued up to EUR 150 and sold in distance sales. This in principle includes books and newspapers.
However, imported goods, including books and newspapers, can benefit from existing duty exemptions or preferential treatment if they fulfil the relevant conditions.

Books and newspapers printed in third countries and meeting the rules of origin with those third countries for which the EU has preferential trade agreements can benefit from preferential duty rates, if the appropriate proof of origin is provided when required to the customs authorities.
Pursuant to the Duty Relief Regulation (1), the duty-free import of certain educational, scientific and cultural materials will still be possible, provided that certain conditions are met.

For example, it will be possible to import duty-free microfilms of books, children’s picture books or colouring books, maps, and scientific charts and diagrams, as long as the advertising contained therein does not cover more than 25% of the surface.

Regulation (EU) 2019/880 regulates more widely the introduction and import of cultural goods into the EU but it generally applies to goods with a minimum value threshold of EUR 18000 and it is therefore not relevant for goods to which the temporary EUR 3 duty applies.
